title: Raspberry Pi IoT Capstone Project
subtitle: End-to-end sensor dashboard: DHT22 → MQTT → InfluxDB → Grafana
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Individual skills — GPIO, MQTT, Python services — are only useful when they come together in a real, working system. Without building an end-to-end project, the connections between components remain abstract.
whyItExists.solution: This capstone project assembles everything into a production-quality IoT dashboard: a physical sensor, a Python data collector, MQTT for messaging, InfluxDB for time-series storage, and Grafana for live visualisation — all running on a single Raspberry Pi.
whyItExists.whenToUse: As a reference architecture for any IoT monitoring system: home environment, industrial equipment, server room, greenhouse, weather station.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: This stack (Mosquitto + InfluxDB + Grafana) needs a Pi 3 or Pi 4 with ≥1 GB RAM. It's too heavy for a Pi Zero. For simple local display, skip InfluxDB/Grafana and use a small OLED directly.

explainModes.beginner: This project connects a temperature sensor to your Pi, stores the readings in a database, and shows them on a beautiful live chart in a web browser. After this, you'll understand how every professional IoT dashboard works under the hood.
explainModes.simple: The pipeline: DHT22 sensor → Python script reads it every 10 seconds → publishes JSON to MQTT broker → Telegraf agent receives MQTT and writes to InfluxDB time-series database → Grafana queries InfluxDB and draws live charts. Each piece is replaceable with alternatives.
explainModes.standard: This follows the standard IoT stack: sensor → edge collector (Python/paho-mqtt) → message bus (MQTT/Mosquitto) → time-series database (InfluxDB 2.x) → visualisation (Grafana). Telegraf is the bridge between MQTT and InfluxDB. The entire stack runs on one Pi or can be distributed across multiple nodes.
explainModes.technical: InfluxDB 2.x uses a bucket/measurement/tag/field model. Telegraf's MQTT consumer input subscribes to topics and parses JSON payload to InfluxDB line protocol. Grafana connects via the InfluxDB data source plugin using Flux query language. Each component exposes health endpoints for monitoring.
explainModes.deepDive: For production scale: use Docker Compose for reproducible deployment and easy upgrades. InfluxDB retention policies automatically purge data older than N days (configure per bucket). Grafana alerting sends notifications to Telegram, Slack, PagerDuty, or email when thresholds are crossed. For multi-Pi setups: Telegraf on each Pi with a central InfluxDB; use InfluxDB's multi-tenancy (organisations + buckets) to separate device streams.

content.text: This capstone project builds a complete IoT monitoring system on a single Raspberry Pi. The data flows through five stages: Sensor → Collector → MQTT → Database → Dashboard. Each stage is a separate process, communicating via standard protocols — making each component replaceable.

content.code:
IoT Dashboard Architecture
──────────────────────────────────────────────

  [DHT22 Sensor]
       │ GPIO4 (physical pin 7)
       ▼
  [Python Collector]          sensor_collector.py
    - reads DHT22 every 10s
    - publishes JSON to MQTT
       │ paho-mqtt
       ▼
  [Mosquitto MQTT Broker]     port 1883
    - routes messages
       │
       ▼
  [Telegraf Agent]            MQTT consumer plugin
    - subscribes to sensor/#
    - writes to InfluxDB
       │ HTTP line protocol
       ▼
  [InfluxDB 2.x]              port 8086  (time-series DB)
    - stores readings
       │ Flux queries
       ▼
  [Grafana]                   port 3000  (dashboard UI)
    - live charts, alerts
    - accessible from browser

# Update system
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

# Install Mosquitto MQTT broker
sudo apt install -y mosquitto mosquitto-clients
sudo systemctl enable --now mosquitto

# Install InfluxDB 2.x (ARM64 — Pi 4/5 or Pi 3 64-bit OS)
curl -s https://repos.influxdata.com/influxdata-archive_compat.key | sudo tee /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/influxdata-archive_compat.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/influxdata-archive_compat.gpg] https://repos.influxdata.com/debian stable main' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/influxdata.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y influxdb2
sudo systemctl enable --now influxd

# Install Telegraf (InfluxDB agent)
sudo apt install -y telegraf

# Install Grafana
sudo apt install -y apt-transport-https software-properties-common wget
sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings/
wget -q -O - https://apt.grafana.com/gpg.key | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.gpg > /dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.gpg] https://apt.grafana.com stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/grafana.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y grafana
sudo systemctl enable --now grafana-server

echo "Stack installed!"
echo "InfluxDB: http://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):8086"
echo "Grafana:  http://$(hostname -I | awk '{print $1}'):3000"

#!/home/pi/iot-dashboard/venv/bin/python
"""DHT22 sensor collector — reads every 10s, publishes to MQTT."""
import adafruit_dht
import board
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json
import time
import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s'
)

DEVICE_ID = "pi-01"
BROKER    = "localhost"
INTERVAL  = 10  # seconds between readings

# DHT22 on GPIO4 (physical pin 7)
dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4)

client = mqtt.Client(mqtt.CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2, f"collector-{DEVICE_ID}")
client.will_set(f"sensors/{DEVICE_ID}/status",
                json.dumps({"online": False, "device": DEVICE_ID}), qos=1, retain=True)
client.connect(BROKER, 1883, keepalive=60)
client.loop_start()

# Announce online
client.publish(f"sensors/{DEVICE_ID}/status",
               json.dumps({"online": True, "device": DEVICE_ID}), qos=1, retain=True)

logging.info(f"Collector started — device={DEVICE_ID}, interval={INTERVAL}s")

while True:
    try:
        temperature = dht.temperature
        humidity    = dht.humidity

        if temperature is not None and humidity is not None:
            payload = {
                "device":      DEVICE_ID,
                "temperature": round(float(temperature), 1),
                "humidity":    round(float(humidity), 1),
                "ts":          int(time.time())
            }
            topic = f"sensors/{DEVICE_ID}/data"
            client.publish(topic, json.dumps(payload), qos=1)
            logging.info(f"Published: {payload}")
        else:
            logging.warning("DHT22 returned None — skipping")

    except RuntimeError as e:
        logging.warning(f"DHT read error: {e}")
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error(f"Unexpected error: {e}")

    time.sleep(INTERVAL)

content.text: Step 3: Configure Telegraf to Bridge MQTT → InfluxDB

content.code:
# /etc/telegraf/telegraf.d/mqtt-sensors.conf

[[inputs.mqtt_consumer]]
  servers  = ["tcp://localhost:1883"]
  topics   = ["sensors/+/data"]
  qos      = 1
  data_format = "json"

  # Map JSON fields to InfluxDB tags and fields
  json_string_fields = ["device"]
  tag_keys = ["device"]

  # Measurement name in InfluxDB
  name_override = "environment"

[[outputs.influxdb_v2]]
  urls   = ["http://localhost:8086"]
  token  = "YOUR_INFLUXDB_TOKEN"   # from InfluxDB UI → Load Data → API Tokens
  org    = "home"
  bucket = "sensors"

# Create project and virtual environment
mkdir -p /home/pi/iot-dashboard
cd /home/pi/iot-dashboard
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install adafruit-circuitpython-dht paho-mqtt adafruit-blinka

# Copy sensor_collector.py here
cp sensor_collector.py /home/pi/iot-dashboard/

# Create systemd service
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/sensor-collector.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=DHT22 Sensor Collector
After=network.target mosquitto.service
Wants=mosquitto.service

[Service]
Type=simple
User=pi
Group=pi
WorkingDirectory=/home/pi/iot-dashboard
ExecStart=/home/pi/iot-dashboard/venv/bin/python sensor_collector.py
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sensor-collector.service
sudo systemctl enable --now telegraf

# Check everything is running
for svc in mosquitto influxd telegraf sensor-collector grafana-server; do
  echo -n "$svc: "
  systemctl is-active $svc
done

content.text: Open Grafana at http://your-pi-ip:3000 (default login: admin/admin — change immediately). Add InfluxDB as a data source (Connections → Data sources → InfluxDB, Flux language). Create a new dashboard with a Time series panel using this Flux query: `from(bucket: "sensors") |> range(start: -1h) |> filter(fn: (r) => r._measurement == "environment") |> filter(fn: (r) => r._field == "temperature")`

InfluxDB 2.x and Grafana each require ~200–400 MB RAM at idle. The full stack (Mosquitto + InfluxDB + Telegraf + Grafana) needs a Raspberry Pi 3B or Pi 4 with ≥1 GB RAM. On a Pi Zero W (512 MB RAM), only run Mosquitto + the Python collector — use a separate machine for InfluxDB and Grafana.

questions.question: What is Telegraf's role in this IoT stack?
options: It is the MQTT broker that routes sensor messages
It bridges MQTT messages to InfluxDB by subscribing to topics and writing data
It is the Python script that reads the DHT22 sensor
questions.explanation: Telegraf is an agent that collects metrics from many sources. Here it uses the mqtt_consumer input plugin to subscribe to MQTT topics and the influxdb_v2 output plugin to write data to InfluxDB — no custom code needed.

questions.question: What role does Grafana play in this IoT stack?
options: It publishes MQTT messages from sensor data
It provides live dashboard visualisation by querying InfluxDB
It runs the Python sensor collector
questions.explanation: Grafana is a visualisation tool. It queries InfluxDB using Flux queries and renders live charts, graphs, and gauges. It doesn't store data itself — InfluxDB does that.

questions.question: Why is a Raspberry Pi Zero W not recommended for running the full stack (InfluxDB + Grafana)?
options: Pi Zero W doesn't support WiFi
InfluxDB and Grafana require ~400–800 MB RAM total — Pi Zero W has only 512 MB
Pi Zero W can't install Python packages
The GPIO pins on Pi Zero W are incompatible with DHT22
questions.explanation: InfluxDB and Grafana each idle at 200–400 MB RAM. The Pi Zero W has only 512 MB total. Running both would leave almost no memory for the OS and sensor scripts, causing swapping, slowness, and crashes.

faq.q: Can a Raspberry Pi Zero W run this full stack?
faq.a: Only partially. The Pi Zero W (1 core, 512 MB RAM) can handle the Python sensor collector and Mosquitto broker. InfluxDB + Grafana together need ~400–800 MB RAM and Pi 3 or Pi 4. For a Zero W deployment, run only Mosquitto on the Pi and use a cloud InfluxDB + Grafana instance.

faq.q: How do I add Grafana alerting to get notified when temperature spikes?
faq.a: In Grafana: open the panel → Edit → Alert tab → Create alert rule. Set threshold (e.g., temperature > 30°C for 2 minutes). Configure a notification channel (Alerting → Contact points) for Telegram, Email, Slack, or PagerDuty. Grafana evaluates the alert every 10–60 seconds and sends notifications on state change.

faq.q: How much disk space does InfluxDB use over time?
faq.a: With 10-second readings and 2 fields: ~100 MB per year per sensor after compression. InfluxDB 2.x supports retention policies per bucket (Buckets → Edit → Set retention period) to automatically delete data older than N days, keeping disk usage bounded.

examples: Home sensor dashboard: Pi 4 running full TIG stack (Telegraf + InfluxDB + Grafana) for 8 rooms, accessible on local network with Grafana alerts to Telegram
Server room monitoring: Pi Zero W per rack → Mosquitto → central Pi 4 InfluxDB + Grafana with cooling alerts
